title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 219: Secrets of the Annual Ring
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 219 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

Secrets of the Annual Ring: Dendroclimatology and Volcanic Cataclysms

Paragraph 1. To ordinary walkers, rings inside a cut tree trunk simply show a tree's age. To climate scientists, however, these wooden circles serve as detailed weather diaries. In regions where cold winter weather pauses tree growth, each tree adds exactly one ring per year. During warm, rainy growing seasons, rings turn out thick and broad; during cold or dry years, growth slows down and leaves thin, narrow lines. By matching living ancient trees with preserved wood from old buildings and ruins, researchers have built unbroken timelines stretching back over ten thousand years.

Paragraph 2. Even more valuable are rare damaged layers known as 'frost rings'. In these unusual bands, wood cells appear crushed and frozen right in the middle of their summer growth cycle. A frost ring marks a sudden, unseasonal freeze striking in midsummer across huge areas of a continent.

Paragraph 3. For years, historians struggled to explain sixth-century reports of a strange dark fog covering Europe, the Mediterranean, and Asia in 536 CE. Writer Procopius observed that the sun shone weakly like the moon for an entire year, while crops failed in Ireland and summer snow fell in China. By examining high-altitude pines in California and larches in Siberia, scientist Dr. Michael Baillie proved that 536 CE brought the worst tree-growth collapse in two thousand years.

Paragraph 4. Scientists later linked these historic cold shocks directly to massive volcanic eruptions. When huge volcanoes explode, they shoot millions of tonnes of sulfur dioxide gas high into the dry upper sky above rain clouds. There, the gas mixes with water vapour to form thin sulfuric acid clouds that circle the globe within weeks. These shiny clouds reflect sunlight back into space, cooling Earth's surface by up to three degrees Celsius for several years.

Paragraph 5. To confirm these dates, researchers compare tree-ring scars with acidic layers trapped inside polar glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica. However, scientist Dr. Valerie Trouet warns that mountain trees mainly record temperature while dry lowland trees mainly record drought. Ultimately, ancient wood proves that the rapid global warming of the last fifty years has no equal in the past ten millennia.

q6.text: The width of an annual tree ring reflects the weather during that growing season.

steps: Đoạn 1: Mùa ấm nhiều mưa thì vòng rộng, lạnh khô thì vòng hẹp.

q7.text: Master tree-ring timelines only go back about two thousand years.

steps: Đoạn 1: Chuỗi niên đại kéo dài hơn 10.000 năm (over ten thousand years), không phải chỉ 2.000 năm.

q8.text: Dr. Valerie Trouet conducted most of her field research on tropical islands.

steps: Đoạn 5: Chỉ nêu cảnh báo chuyên môn của Dr. Trouet, không nhắc bà làm nghiên cứu ở đảo nhiệt đới.

q9.text: Trees growing in dry lowland areas give the best measurement of summer temperatures.

steps: Đoạn 5: Cây vùng đất thấp khô hạn đo hạn hán (drought), còn cây núi cao mới đo nhiệt độ.
